summary: This document defines DHCP and IPv6 Router Advertisement options that tell a host about encrypted DNS resolvers provided by its network. A host learns an authentication domain name, a list of IP addresses, and service parameters, for resolvers using DNS over HTTPS, DNS over TLS, or DNS over QUIC.

plainLanguage.summary:
When a computer joins a network, it usually learns the address of the network's DNS resolver, the machine that turns names into addresses. That is not enough to set up an encrypted DNS connection, because the computer also needs a name it can check the resolver's certificate against.

RFC 9463 adds three options that carry that name, the resolver's IP addresses and the parameters of the service. A host then knows both where to connect and what to expect.

questions: dhcp option for doh and dot
subtitle: DHCP and IPv6 Router Advertisement options that let a network tell hosts where its encrypted DNS resolvers are.

tldr.problem: Hosts joining a network normally learn only the IP address of its DNS resolver, which is not enough to set up DoH, DoT or DoQ with proper authentication.
tldr.mechanism: New DHCPv4, DHCPv6 and IPv6 Router Advertisement options carry an Authentication Domain Name, a list of IP addresses and service parameters encoded as SvcParams.
tldr.outcome: A host can connect to the network's encrypted resolver without extra lookups and authenticate it by name. The options are not themselves protected, so local spoofing must be mitigated separately.

today: RFC 9463 was published in November 2023 and is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works alongside RFC 9462, and its options take precedence over DDR when both are present.

sections.title: What DNR Does
sections.content:
This document is about finding encrypted DNS resolvers in a local network. A resolver is an encrypted one when it speaks DNS over HTTPS (DoH), DNS over TLS (DoT) or DNS over QUIC (DoQ), so that DNS traffic travels over an encrypted channel.

It specifies three ways for a host to learn about such a resolver: a DHCPv4 option, a DHCPv6 option and an IPv6 Router Advertisement option. All three carry the same three pieces of information: the DNS Authentication Domain Name, a list of IP addresses, and a set of service parameters. The whole procedure is called Discovery of Network-designated Resolvers (DNR).

The options are meant to work in many kinds of deployment, from local networks whose equipment is managed by an internet service provider to home networks with a plain DNS forwarder. Resolver selection and the policies around it, including how the user is consulted, are outside the scope of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer joining a network needs to find the network's encrypted DNS resolver and be able to check that it is talking to the right one. This RFC adds three options, one for each way a host learns its network settings, and all three carry the same information.

sections.title: The Configuration Data
sections.content:
The options always carry an Authentication Domain Name, a name the client uses to authenticate the resolver. It is included so that the resolver's certificate can be checked against a name rather than against an IP address, which follows the current practice for issuing certificates.

They also carry the IP addresses of the resolver, so that the client does not have to ask another server to look up the name first. The addresses may be on the same address or on different ones, and a list can be returned to accommodate a primary and a backup resolver. When several are returned they are ordered by preference. The address can be a private IPv4 address, a link-local address, an IPv6 Unique Local Address or a Global Unicast Address.

The third piece is a set of service parameters, encoded in the same way as the SvcParams of RFC 9460. This lets the network name the protocols the resolver supports and, if needed, a non-default port. Every implementation MUST support the alpn parameter, which lists the supported protocols, and the port parameter, which gives the target port. The dohpath parameter, which supplies a relative DoH URI template, is RECOMMENDED. The ipv4hint and ipv6hint parameters MUST NOT be included, because the option already lists the addresses.

One option carries both the name and the addresses rather than two separate options, because otherwise a way of correlating an address in one option with a name in another would be needed, and a network may offer more than one name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each option carries three things: the name to authenticate the resolver against, the resolver's IP addresses in preference order, and the parameters of the service such as the protocols it speaks and the port to use. Keeping the name and the addresses in one option avoids having to work out which name goes with which address.

sections.title: Conflicts with Other Discovery
sections.content:
If a host learns about encrypted DNS resolvers from both a router advertisement and DHCP, the rules of Section 5.3.1 of RFC 8106 apply. The DHCP and router advertisement options take precedence over Discovery of Designated Resolvers, DDR, described in RFC 9462, because DDR uses unencrypted DNS to an external resolver, which is open to attacks from inside and outside, while the DHCP and router advertisement options are typically protected by the mechanisms the RFC describes.

If a client learns about both an unencrypted resolver and encrypted resolvers from the same network, and is not configured otherwise, it is RECOMMENDED that the client use the encrypted resolvers. If the client cannot establish an authenticated and encrypted connection to the encrypted resolver, it may fall back to the unencrypted one.

Other provisioning mechanisms may be needed where DHCP and router advertisements are not available or not secure enough. The RFC says that at least a service priority, a name, a list of addresses and a set of service parameters should be made available to the host by whatever mechanism is used. The name is the one mandatory item.
sections.plainLanguage: When a host gets resolver information from both DHCP and a router advertisement, the DHCP and advertisement options win over the older mechanism that looks up a resolver by unencrypted DNS. If a host learns of both encrypted and unencrypted resolvers, it should prefer the encrypted one, but may fall back if the encrypted connection cannot be made.

sections.title: Client Behavior and Validation
sections.content:
When an option arrives, the client checks that the name is present and encoded as required. If extra data is present, it also checks that the service parameters are encoded correctly, that there is at least one valid IP address, and that the parameters do not include the address hint parameters. If any check fails, the client discards the option.

The client must be ready to receive several instances, and treats each as a separate resolver, processing them in order of service priority, where a smaller value means a higher preference. The client must silently discard any option that fails the validation checks, and it must silently discard multicast addresses and host loopback addresses that appear in the option.

To confirm that a discovered resolver is the one the network meant, the client verifies the connection using PKIX validation of the resolver's certificate and compares the name from the option with the certificate, using the validation techniques of RFC 6125. It uses the system or application trust anchors unless it has been configured with explicit ones. These checks confirm that the resolver matches what was advertised; they do not judge the security of the provisioning mechanism or the user's trust in the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using an option, the host checks that it is well formed and that it carries at least one usable address. It then connects to the resolver and checks the resolver's certificate against the name from the option. An option that fails any check is thrown away silently.

sections.title: The Three Options
sections.content:
The DHCPv6 option has code 144, OPTION_V6_DNR. After the option code and length come a 16-bit service priority, the length of the name and the name itself, then the length of the addresses and the addresses, then the service parameters. When only a name is carried, the option length is the name length plus four. The address length must be a multiple of 16.

The DHCPv4 option has code 162, OPTION_V4_DNR. Its body is a list of instances, each holding an instance length, a 16-bit service priority, the name, the addresses and the service parameters. The instance length is the name length plus three when only a name is present, and the address length must be a multiple of 4. This option requires the concatenation mechanism of RFC 3396 if it exceeds the maximum DHCPv4 option size of 255 octets.

The IPv6 Router Advertisement option is a Neighbor Discovery option of type 144. It carries a type and a length in units of eight octets, a 16-bit service priority, a 32-bit lifetime in seconds, the name, the addresses and the service parameters. The lifetime should by default be at least three times the maximum router advertisement interval; a value of all one bits means infinity, and a value of zero means the name must no longer be used. The option is padded with zeros so that the enclosed data is a multiple of eight octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The DHCPv6 and DHCPv4 options carry the name, the addresses and the parameters directly. The router advertisement option carries the same things plus a lifetime, and its length field counts eight octets at a time. All three can carry more than one resolver, each with its own priority.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DHCP and router advertisement messages are not encrypted and are not protected against modification inside the local network. An active attacker can spoof the response and point the host at the attacker's own encrypted resolver, which is easy to set up because a certificate for a domain name can be obtained from a public authority. The RFC names three mitigations that a network access node can apply: DHCPv6-Shield of RFC 7610, which discards DHCP responses that arrive from a local endpoint; RA-Guard of RFC 7113, which does the same for router advertisements; and the Source Address Validation Improvement solution for DHCP of RFC 7513, which filters packets with forged source addresses. These mechanisms ensure the host gets the configuration the network intended, but they say nothing about who is running the DHCP server.

Even with spoofing, a session with a rogue resolver fails, because the client checks the certificate against the name from the option and the rogue resolver does not hold a certificate for that name. A client that ignores authentication failures is open to attacks that redirect queries or intercept data.

If the attacker drops the messages instead, the client falls back to a preconfigured resolver. A passive attacker can see that a host uses DHCP or router advertisements to find an encrypted resolver, and can infer that the host supports encrypted DNS, but cannot change anything. On wireless networks, where only cryptographically authenticated communication is trusted, the information in DHCP and router advertisement messages is untrusted, and shared pre-shared keys make on-path attacks possible, so unique credentials per device are needed. The privacy section adds that the options reveal no more than the older unencrypted DNS discovery options do.
sections.plainLanguage: The options travel in the clear inside the local network, so someone on that network could point a host at a resolver of their own. The network can block that with DHCPv6-Shield, RA-Guard and source address checks. The name in the option still protects the host, because a fake resolver will not hold a certificate for that name.

sections.title: The Assigned Codes
sections.content:
Three codes are assigned by IANA. The DHCPv6 option code 144 is registered in the "Option Codes" registry, with "Yes" in the Client ORO column and "No" in the Singleton Option column, meaning a client may request it and may receive more than one instance.

The DHCPv4 option code 162 is registered in the "BOOTP Vendor Extensions and DHCP Options" registry, with a data length of N and the meaning "Encrypted DNS Server".

The IPv6 Neighbor Discovery option type 144 is registered in the "IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Option Formats" subregistry, with the description "Encrypted DNS Option".
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the three mechanisms gets its own number: 144 for DHCPv6, 162 for DHCPv4, and 144 again for the IPv6 router advertisement option.

items.title: Authentication Domain Name
items.text: The name the client checks the resolver's certificate against.

items.title: IP addresses
items.text: One or more, in preference order; private, link-local, ULA or global.

items.title: Service parameters
items.text: Encoded as SvcParams: alpn for the protocols, port for the target port, dohpath for the DoH template.

items.title: Service priority
items.text: A 16-bit number; a smaller value means a higher preference.

fields.name: Option Length
fields.desc: Length of the enclosed data in octets.

fields.name: Service Priority
fields.desc: Priority of this resolver against the others.

fields.name: ADN Length
fields.desc: Length of the authentication domain name in octets.

fields.name: authentication-domain-name
fields.desc: The fully qualified domain name of the resolver.

fields.name: Addr Length
fields.desc: Length of the enclosed IPv6 addresses; a multiple of 16.

fields.name: ipv6-address(es)
fields.desc: One or more IPv6 addresses of the resolver.

fields.name: Service Parameters
fields.desc: SvcParams as encoded in RFC 9460; should include alpn.
